title: Sons, Health and Slaves
sum: Ben Sira finishes his teaching on raising sons: love means discipline, and a well-trained son keeps his father's name alive after death (30:1–13). Then he praises health above wealth, and joy above grief: a glad heart is a man's life, and worry ages him before his time (30:14–24).

After 30:24 the Greek manuscripts jump to a block that the Hebrew, the Latin and the KJV place three chapters later (KJV 33:16–31). Ben Sira calls himself a late gleaner who still filled a winepress, and tells the leaders of the people to keep control of their property until death and to run their households firmly. His advice on slaves is harsh (stick, rack, shackles) and then turns: treat a slave like yourself, for you need him as your own life (30:25–40).
readings: Read as advice for its time

Ben Sira writes for wealthy heads of household in Jerusalem: men with sons to raise, estates to keep and slaves to manage. Read this way, the chapter is a window on that world, its fears (a son out of control, a father dependent on his heirs, a runaway slave) and its remedies.
Read for its lasting wisdom

Under the ancient customs lie lasting points: love disciplines (Hebrews 12:5–11); health and a glad heart are worth more than money (Proverbs 17:22); do not give up your independence too soon; a servant is a person to treat 'like yourself'. Catholic and Orthodox readers, for whom the book is Scripture, read it this way, and so do many Protestants who read it as wise counsel.

views.C: The Catholic Church counts Sirach among the inspired books, but reads its household rules, as it reads the Old Testament's laws on slavery, in the light of the Gospel and of its own teaching on human dignity.
views.O: The Orthodox churches read Sirach as part of the Old Testament they received in Greek.
views.P: Protestants place Sirach among the Apocrypha. Its sayings on discipline and on health are read as sound advice that agrees with Proverbs; its rules for slaves are read as history, not as teaching.
views.H: Historical-critical readers note the transposition of the blocks after 30:24 and check the Greek against the Hebrew: MS B from the Cairo Genizah covers 30:11–24, and damaged lines of MS E cover 30:25–40.
views.J: The Hebrew of 30:11–24 survives in MS B, a medieval copy from the Cairo Genizah, so Jews were still copying these sayings long after Ben Sira. The Talmud (Sanhedrin 100b) quotes a saying close to 30:23 on worry, and Rav Yosef there allows the good parts of the book to be taught.

echoes: Proverbs 13:24; Proverbs 23:13–14; Proverbs 17:22; Ephesians 6:4; Hebrews 12:5–11; Luke 15:12; Exodus 21:20–27; Deuteronomy 15:12–15; Job 31:13–15; Philemon 1:16; Ruth 2:2–3

settings.to: Fathers among his hearers, heads of households
settings.when: in his teaching on family life
settings.why: To persuade fathers that firm discipline, even the rod, is love, because a son left loose ruins his father's old age and name. Knowing the hearers were wealthy men whose sons would inherit estates and positions shows the stakes: an undisciplined heir could shame or ruin a family.
settings.readers: Ben Sira's students in Jerusalem, the young men of his "house of instruction" (51:23), between about 190 and 170 BC (Gigot's date); then the Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt for whom his grandson translated the book after he came there in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes (the prologue), 132 BC by Gigot's reckoning. The Hebrew of 30:11–13 is in the medieval Cairo Genizah manuscript B (folio III recto).

settings.what: Health, food and the glad heart
settings.why: To set health and joy above wealth, and to warn against grief and worry. Rich young men are reminded that a sick rich man is worse off than a healthy poor one.
settings.readers: The same first readers (see the first setting on this page). The Hebrew of these verses is in MS B (folio III recto and the first line of III verso), and the Babylonian Talmud discusses a saying close to 30:23 (Sanhedrin 100b).

settings.what: Ben Sira on his own work
settings.to: The great men of the people and the leaders of the assembly
settings.when: in the Hebrew order, just after the teaching on God's pairs of opposites (36:14–15 here)
settings.why: To claim authority for his teaching: though he came late, after Israel's great teachers, the Lord blessed his gleaning, and he labored for all who seek instruction. Knowing that he addresses Jerusalem's leaders explains the advice that follows on property and household.
settings.readers: Addressed in the text to "the great men of the people" and "you leaders of the assembly" (30:27). The Hebrew is in damaged lines of MS E (folio I verso, lines 3–6).

settings.to: The leaders of 30:27: men with estates and household slaves
settings.why: To teach a property owner to keep control of his goods until death (so he is not left begging his heirs) and to run his household firmly but not cruelly. The slave rules bind the master, not the slave; they assume the slave-owning society of Hellenistic Judea, and they end with the reminder that the slave is a person 'like yourself'.
settings.readers: Owners of estates and household slaves, by the text's own address (30:27; 30:39). The Hebrew is in damaged lines of MS E (folio I verso, lines 7–20).

title: Dreams, Travel and True Worship
sum: This chapter (KJV 34) opens with a warning: dreams and omens are empty, a shadow or a reflection, unless the Most High sends them; the law is sure (31:1–8). Ben Sira then speaks of his own travels: the man who has wandered and been tested knows much, and he himself came near death many times. The fear of the Lord keeps such a man safe (31:9–20).

The rest of the chapter is a sharp word against worship without justice. An offering from stolen goods is a mockery; bringing a sacrifice out of what belongs to the poor is like killing a son before his father's eyes; holding back a worker's pay is shedding blood. Washing after touching a corpse and then touching it again is useless; so is fasting for your sins and going back to them (31:21–31).
readings: Read as a prophet's word

31:21–31 stands with Amos, Isaiah and Micah: God wants justice before sacrifice. Read this way, it is a strong social passage from outside the Hebrew Bible, and 31:21 is the verse that turned Bartolomé de las Casas against the treatment of native peoples in 1514.
Read as a scribe's experience

The first half is the voice of a learned man who has traveled and seen the world's superstitions. He trusts the law and the fear of the Lord, not dreams. Read this way, the chapter shows Jewish wisdom meeting the Greek world's diviners and dream-readers with calm confidence.

views.C: Catholic readers know 31:21 (KJV 34:18) through Las Casas, whose change of heart began with it. Catholic social teaching makes the same points about fair wages and the poor.
views.O: Its warning about fasting without change (31:31) fits the Orthodox churches' long tradition of fasting joined to repentance.
views.P: Protestants hear in 31:21–31 the voice of the prophets; many quote 31:25–27 on wages and the poor beside James 5:4. On dreams, the chapter agrees with the Reformers' caution about private revelations.
views.H: Historical-critical readers read 31:1–8 beside the dream books and oracles of the Hellenistic world. They compare 31:21–31 with the prophets and note that Ben Sira, a lover of the temple (50:1–21), is not against sacrifice but against injustice behind it.
views.J: Of this chapter only the first line survives in Hebrew, damaged, at the foot of MS E. The Talmud makes Ben Sira's point with the same picture: confessing a sin without leaving it is like immersing in a ritual bath while holding something unclean in your hand (Taanit 16a).

echoes: Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 18:10–14; Jeremiah 23:25–28; Ecclesiastes 5:7; Job 14:4; Psalm 33:18; Psalm 121:3–6; Isaiah 1:11–17; Amos 5:21–24; Proverbs 15:8; Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15; James 5:4; Numbers 19:11–22; Isaiah 58:3–7; 2 Peter 2:22

settings.why: To steer young men away from the diviners and dream-interpreters common in the Hellenistic world, and toward the law as the sure guide. Dreams sent by God are not denied (31:6), but they are rare.
settings.readers: Ben Sira's students in Jerusalem, the young men of his "house of instruction" (51:23), between about 190 and 170 BC (Gigot's date); then the Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt for whom his grandson translated the book after he came there in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes (the prologue), 132 BC by Gigot's reckoning. Only the first line of this chapter survives in Hebrew, damaged, at the foot of MS E (folio I verso, line 21).

settings.what: Travel, testing and the fear of the Lord
settings.by: Ben Sira, speaking partly of himself
settings.why: To show that experience, testing and travel make a man wise, and that the one who fears the Lord is safe in danger. Ben Sira's own brushes with death (31:13) give the lesson weight.
settings.readers: The same first readers (see the first setting on this page). No Hebrew manuscript read for this site has these verses.

settings.to: Worshipers at the Jerusalem temple, especially the wealthy who could afford large offerings
settings.when: in the years when the temple stood and its sacrifices were offered daily
settings.why: To warn the rich that God refuses offerings paid for by cheating the poor, withholding wages or taking a neighbor's living, and that ritual washing or fasting is useless without a change of life. The hearers were the very men who could build fortunes on others' labor and then make large gifts at the temple.
settings.readers: The same first readers (see the first setting on this page). No Hebrew manuscript read for this site has these verses. Bartolomé de las Casas came upon 31:21 while preparing a Pentecost sermon in 1514 (U.S. Catholic).

title: The Offering God Accepts
sum: This chapter (KJV 35) joins the law and the altar. Keeping the law is a full offering; repaying kindness is a grain offering; giving alms is a sacrifice of praise; turning from wrong makes atonement (32:1–5). Yet the offerings still matter: do not come before the Lord with empty hands, give with a glad face and a good eye, for the Lord repays seven times over (32:6–13).

Then God is the judge who cannot be bribed and does not play favorites. He hears the orphan and the widow; the prayer of the humble goes through the clouds and will not rest until he acts. He will not delay or be patient with the merciless, until he repays the nations and makes his people glad with his mercy (32:14–26). Luke's parable of the widow and the unjust judge uses the same picture and the same Greek phrase (Luke 18:1–8).
readings: Read as teaching on worship

Ben Sira holds together what later debates often pulled apart: the outward offering and the inward life. Good deeds are 'sacrifices', but the actual sacrifices are still commanded. Hebrews 13:15–16 makes the same move for Christians.
Read as hope for the oppressed

From 32:14 the chapter is a promise to the poor, the orphan and the widow that God the judge hears them, and a threat to the oppressors and the nations. Read with Luke 18, it is the Jewish background of Jesus' call to pray and not lose heart.

views.C: The Catholic lectionary reads this chapter (numbered Sirach 35 in its Bibles): on Tuesday of the 8th week in Ordinary Time in Year I, and the passage on the prayer of the lowly (35:12–14, 16–18 there) on the 30th Sunday in Ordinary Time, Year C.
views.O: Orthodox teaching on almsgiving and prayer as offerings to God fits 32:1–5.
views.P: Protestants read 32:1–5 as the prophets' teaching that God wants obedience more than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22), and 32:14–26 as a witness to God's justice that Jesus' parable confirms; they do not take 32:5 as a ground of forgiveness apart from Christ.
views.H: Historical-critical readers see Ben Sira holding law-keeping and temple worship together rather than setting them against each other. They compare 32:14–26 with Luke 18:1–8, where the shared Greek phrase (makrothymeō ep' autois) may mean that Luke's readers knew the passage or the tradition behind it.
views.J: The Hebrew of 32:11–26 survives in MS B (folio VI recto) from the Cairo Genizah. The idea that deeds of kindness stand in for sacrifice became central in rabbinic Judaism after the temple fell in AD 70.

echoes: 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Psalm 50:14; Hebrews 13:15–16; Leviticus 2:1–2; Deuteronomy 16:16–17; 2 Corinthians 9:7; Tobit 4:8; Deuteronomy 10:17–18; Exodus 22:22–24; Luke 18:1–8; Psalm 62:12; Romans 2:6; Romans 2:11

settings.to: Jewish worshipers who brought offerings at the temple
settings.when: while the temple service went on
settings.why: To teach that obedience and kindness are themselves offerings, and that the commanded offerings must still be brought gladly and generously. The hearers had the means to give; Ben Sira wants them to give freely and to live justly.
settings.readers: Ben Sira's students in Jerusalem, the young men of his "house of instruction" (51:23), between about 190 and 170 BC (Gigot's date); then the Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt for whom his grandson translated the book after he came there in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes (the prologue), 132 BC by Gigot's reckoning. No Hebrew manuscript read for this site covers 32:1–10; MS B resumes at 32:11 (folio VI recto).

settings.what: God the judge hears the widow
settings.to: His hearers, both the powerful and the poor among them
settings.when: in a land under foreign rule (32:23)
settings.why: To assure the wronged, the orphan and the widow that God hears them, and to warn the merciless that he will not wait forever. Knowing that Judea was ruled by foreign kings (Gigot places Ben Sira in the time of Simon II, about 200 BC) explains the turn from the oppressor to the nations, and leads into the prayer of chapter 33.
settings.readers: The same first readers (see the first setting on this page). The Hebrew of these verses is in MS B (folio VI recto).
views: The parable in Luke 18:1–8 shares this passage's widow, its persistent prayer and the phrase 'be patient with them'; Luke's first readers, Greek-speaking Christians, may have known Ben Sira's words.

title: Gather the Tribes of Jacob
sum: A prayer for Israel bursts out of the teaching: have mercy on us, Master, God of all; raise your hand over the nations and let them know, as we know, that there is no God but you. Renew your signs and wonders as at the exodus; rouse your anger against the enemy; hurry the time and remember your oath; smash the heads of the rulers who say, 'There is no one but us' (33:1–12).

The chapter is only thirteen verses long, because the Greek manuscripts break the prayer off after 'Gather all the tribes of Jacob' (33:13). It resumes at 36:16 with 'you will give them their inheritance as at the beginning' and goes on to Israel the firstborn, Jerusalem and the prophets (36:16–22). In the KJV the whole prayer is 36:1–17.
readings: Read as a national prayer

The prayer asks God to act for Israel as he did in the exodus, and to humble the empires that rule it. Its words come from Exodus 15, Ezekiel 36 and Isaiah. Read this way, it is a window on Jewish hope under foreign rule before the Maccabean revolt.
Read as a prayer for the nations
The goal is that the nations 'know you, just as we have known' (33:5). Read this way, the prayer is not only for Israel's revenge but for God to be known by all, a theme that ends it too (36:22).

views.C: The Catholic lectionary reads this prayer (numbered Sirach 36 in its Bibles) on Wednesday of the 8th week in Ordinary Time, Year I.
views.P: Protestants read the prayer as Jewish piety of the time between the Testaments; its hope for the gathering of the tribes is taken up in Matthew 19:28 and John 11:52.
views.H: Historical-critical readers date the prayer with the book (Gigot: between about 190 and 170 BC) and read it against the powers that ruled Judea. They note how the Greek order splits it, and read it whole in the Hebrew of MS B (folio VI verso).
views.J: The Hebrew of the prayer survives in MS B from the Cairo Genizah. Its themes (gathering the tribes of Jacob, Jerusalem, God known by all nations) are the hopes of the prophets (Isaiah 11:12; Isaiah 49:6).

echoes: Exodus 15:6; Ezekiel 36:23; Ezekiel 38:23; Isaiah 45:21; 1 Kings 8:60; Habakkuk 2:3; Isaiah 47:8; Numbers 24:17; Isaiah 11:12; Isaiah 49:6; Matthew 19:28; John 11:52

settings.by: Ben Sira, praying for the people
settings.to: God, the Master of all, in the hearing of Ben Sira's students and readers
settings.when: in a time of foreign rule over Judea, when many of Jacob's tribes were still scattered
settings.why: To ask God to show his power to the nations, to punish the oppressors and to gather all Israel, so that the nations will know there is no God but him. For his students the prayer joined their study of wisdom to the hope of Israel's restoration. It continues at 36:16–22.
settings.readers: Ben Sira's students in Jerusalem, the young men of his "house of instruction" (51:23), between about 190 and 170 BC (Gigot's date); then the Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt for whom his grandson translated the book after he came there in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes (the prologue), 132 BC by Gigot's reckoning. The Hebrew of the prayer is in MS B (folio VI verso, lines 1–9).

title: Wealth, Table Manners and Wine
sum: This chapter (KJV 31) begins with the worries of wealth: the rich man lies awake over his money, the love of gold ruins many, and a rich man who stays blameless, who could have done wrong and did not, is a marvel (34:1–11).

Then Ben Sira teaches a young man how to behave at a great man's table: do not gobble or grab, judge your neighbor's wishes by your own, stop first, eat little and sleep well (34:12–24). On wine he is balanced: it is like life itself if drunk in measure, made to make people glad, but too much brings anger, fights and wounds; and at a wine party, never shame your neighbor or dun him for a debt (34:25–31).
readings: Read as manners
Much of the chapter is etiquette for a young scribe moving among the rich: how to eat, drink and speak at their banquets. It reflects the Greek-style banquets of Jerusalem's upper class.
Read as moral teaching

Under the manners lie moral points: greed is idolatry (34:7), the 'evil eye' of envy (34:13), love of neighbor at the table (34:15), and the right use of God's gifts (34:27). Jesus' own table teaching (Luke 14:7–14) is often compared with it.

views.C: Catholic teaching on temperance, one of the four cardinal virtues, asks for the same measure that 34:27–28 praises: wine as God's good gift, used with restraint.
views.O: Orthodox tradition blesses wine and uses it in the Eucharist; 34:27 fits that use.
views.P: Protestants read the chapter as practical wisdom. Churches that have urged abstinence from alcohol point to the warnings of 34:29–31; others point to the praise of moderate drinking in 34:27–28.
views.H: Toy and Lévi, in the Jewish Encyclopedia, take the banquets Ben Sira describes, with conversation, music and "masters" of the feast, as Greek rather than Hebrew customs. The Hebrew of the chapter survives in MS B (folios III verso to IV verso) and, for 34:24–31, MS F.
views.J: The Hebrew of this chapter, including the word mamon (34:8) and 'know your neighbor as yourself' (34:15), survives in MS B from the Cairo Genizah. Rabbinic tradition kept rules for behavior at meals and the blessing after eating (Deuteronomy 8:10).

echoes: Luke 12:16–21; Ecclesiastes 5:12; 1 Timothy 6:9–10; Matthew 6:24; Mark 10:23–27; Proverbs 23:1–3; Mark 14:20; Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 7:12; Luke 10:8; Isaiah 5:22; Psalm 104:15; Judges 9:13; Proverbs 23:29–35; Ephesians 5:18

settings.what: The worries and dangers of wealth
settings.why: To warn heirs of fortunes that the love of gold ruins, and that honest wealth is rare and praiseworthy. The hearers would soon handle money and power themselves.
settings.readers: Ben Sira's students in Jerusalem, the young men of his "house of instruction" (51:23), between about 190 and 170 BC (Gigot's date); then the Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt for whom his grandson translated the book after he came there in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes (the prologue), 132 BC by Gigot's reckoning. The Hebrew is in MS B (folio III verso).

settings.what: Rules for the banquet and for wine
settings.to: A young man invited to the tables of the great
settings.when: as he enters the social life of the upper class
settings.why: To train a future scribe and official to behave well among the rich: self-control, consideration for others and moderation with wine. Good manners were part of a career; Ben Sira grounds them in love of neighbor and the fear of the Lord.
settings.readers: The same first readers (see the first setting on this page). The Hebrew is in MS B (folios IV recto and IV verso), and from 34:24 also in MS F (folio I recto).

title: The Banquet and the Law
sum: Ben Sira continues at the banquet (KJV 32). If you are made leader of the feast, do not puff yourself up: serve the guests and then sit down. Let the elders speak with knowledge but not over the music, which is a jewel in a gold setting; let the young speak little and only when asked; go home in good time and bless the Maker who fills you with good things (35:1–13).

Then the theme turns to the law. Those who fear the Lord accept discipline and find favor; the seeker of the law is filled with it, the hypocrite is snared by it; the sinner dodges correction. Do nothing without counsel, watch your step, and trust the law and the Lord, for they will not let you down (35:14–24).
readings: Read as wisdom for social life
The banquet rules teach humility, restraint in speech and gratitude. They fit the Greek-style banquets of Jerusalem's elite, and they end, like a Jewish meal, with blessing God (35:13).
Read as wisdom for the life of faith

The second half sets the law at the center: it fills those who seek it and trips those who play at it. Read with the first half, it says that the same fear of the Lord governs the dinner table and the whole of life.

views.C: The Catholic lectionary's Tuesday reading in the 8th week of Year I (its Sirach 35) comes from the next chapter here (32).
views.O: Orthodox readers see in 35:13 the pattern of thanksgiving at every meal.
views.P: Protestants read the banquet rules beside Jesus' teaching on the lowest seat (Luke 14:7–11) and the advice on speech beside James 1:19; the praise of the law (35:24) beside Psalm 119.
views.H: Toy and Lévi, in the Jewish Encyclopedia, see in banquets like those of 35:1–6, with music and a master of the feast, customs taken from Greek society. The Hebrew of MS B, MS E and MS F helps with puzzling Greek lines (35:18, 35:22–23).
views.J: The Hebrew of the chapter survives in MS B, MS E and MS F from the Cairo Genizah. The blessing after the meal (35:13) matches the Jewish practice based on Deuteronomy 8:10.

echoes: John 2:8–10; Luke 14:7–11; Luke 22:26; Isaiah 5:12; Proverbs 10:19; Proverbs 17:28; James 1:19; Deuteronomy 8:10; Psalm 23:5; Proverbs 8:17; Proverbs 15:22; Tobit 4:18; Proverbs 4:23

settings.to: Guests at banquets: the leader of the feast, the elders and the young men
settings.when: at the drinking parties of Jerusalem's upper class
settings.why: To teach humility, service and restraint in speech, and to end the party with thanks to God. Knowing that these were Greek-style banquets shows Ben Sira accepting the customs of his time while keeping them under the fear of the Lord.
settings.readers: Ben Sira's students in Jerusalem, the young men of his "house of instruction" (51:23), between about 190 and 170 BC (Gigot's date); then the Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt for whom his grandson translated the book after he came there in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes (the prologue), 132 BC by Gigot's reckoning. The Hebrew is in MS B (folio V recto) and MS F (folio I recto and verso).

settings.why: To show that the law fills the sincere seeker and exposes the hypocrite, and to urge careful, advised action. The young men would face decisions in public life; Ben Sira points them to counsel, care and trust in the law and the Lord.
settings.readers: The same first readers (see the first setting on this page). The Hebrew is in MS B (folio V verso), MS E (folio I recto) and MS F (folio I verso).

title: God's Pairs and the Prayer's End
sum: The wise man trusts the law, which is as sure as an oracle (36:1–6). Why is one day holy and another ordinary, when all get their light from the sun? Because the Lord set them apart, and in the same way he set people apart: all are clay, but like a potter he blesses some, brings some near and casts others down. All his works come in pairs, good against evil, life against death (36:7–15).

At 36:16 the two swapped blocks meet, and the prayer for Israel begun at 33:1 resumes: have mercy on the people called by your name, Israel your firstborn, and on Jerusalem the city of your rest; fulfill the prophecies; hear us, so that all the earth may know you are God of the ages (36:16–22). The chapter ends with sayings on taste and choice: as the tongue tells foods apart, a wise heart tells lies; a good wife is a man's first gain, a helper and a pillar, and without her he wanders like Cain (36:23–31).
readings: Read as a theology of election

36:7–15 is one of the clearest statements before Paul that God chooses: some days, some people, as a potter shapes clay. Romans 9:21 uses the same picture. Read beside 15:11–20, Ben Sira holds God's choosing and human free will together without explaining how.
Read as a book of pairs

The chapter itself moves in pairs: the wise man and the hypocrite, holy days and ordinary days, blessed and cursed, the prayer's Israel and the nations, a good wife and a homeless man. Ben Sira teaches that seeing these pairs is part of wisdom.

views.C: The Catholic lectionary's Wednesday reading in the 8th week of Year I includes 36:16–22 here. Catholic teaching holds together God's providence and human freedom, the two things 36:13 and 15:14 set side by side.
views.O: Orthodox teaching on synergy, God's grace working with human freedom, is one frame in which 36:13 is read.
views.P: Reformed readers have seen in 36:13 an early statement of the potter's right that Paul uses in Romans 9:21; Arminian and Wesleyan readers stress Jeremiah 18, where the clay can be reworked. Protestants read the book as wisdom, not Scripture, and do not ground doctrine on it.
views.H: Historical-critical readers note Ben Sira's pairs of opposites (36:14–15; 42:24) beside the two ways of Deuteronomy 30. They note that 36:16 is the seam where the swapped blocks meet (Toy and Lévi explain the blocks as two sheets interchanged in an early copy), and read the prayer and the sayings in the Hebrew of MS B.
views.J: The Hebrew of 36:1–31 survives in MS B, with parts also in MS C, D, E and F, all from the Cairo Genizah. Its use of Cain's words (36:30) shows how closely Ben Sira wrote from the Torah.

echoes: Exodus 28:30; Numbers 27:21; James 1:6–8; Jeremiah 5:8; Genesis 1:14; Genesis 2:3; Romans 14:5; Genesis 2:7; Jeremiah 18:6; Isaiah 45:9; Wisdom of Solomon 15:7; Romans 9:21; Ecclesiastes 7:14; Exodus 4:22; Psalm 132:14; Numbers 6:24–27; Job 12:11; Genesis 2:18; Proverbs 18:22; Proverbs 31:26; Genesis 4:12; Luke 9:58

settings.what: The law and God's ordering of the world
settings.why: To ground trust in the law and to explain why God treats days and people differently: he is the Creator who orders all things in pairs. For young men in a Greek-influenced city, it answers the question why Israel and its holy days are set apart.
settings.readers: Ben Sira's students in Jerusalem, the young men of his "house of instruction" (51:23), between about 190 and 170 BC (Gigot's date); then the Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt for whom his grandson translated the book after he came there in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes (the prologue), 132 BC by Gigot's reckoning. The Hebrew of 36:1–3 is in MS B (folio V verso), of 36:1–15 in damaged lines of MS E (folio I recto and verso), and of 36:1–8 in MS F (folio I verso).

settings.by: Ben Sira, praying for the people
settings.to: God, the Lord of the ages
settings.why: To ask God to restore the tribes, show mercy to Israel and Jerusalem, fulfill the prophets' words and answer as the priestly blessing promised, so that all the earth will know him.
settings.readers: The same first readers (see the first setting on this page). The Hebrew is in MS B (folio VI verso, lines 9–16); the first half of 36:16 is also in MS E (folio I verso, line 3).

settings.what: Taste, discernment and choosing a wife
settings.why: To teach discernment, in food, in words and above all in choosing a wife, and to praise marriage as a man's foundation. The hearers were young men whose marriages their families would arrange; Ben Sira urges them to value kindness and a gentle tongue.
settings.readers: The same first readers (see the first setting on this page). The Hebrew is in MS B (folios VI verso and VII recto); 36:27–31 are also in MS C (folio VIII) and 36:29–31 in MS D (folio II recto).
